newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia workers wait for pay after protests.
newsitem.headline: Russia workers wait for pay after protests.

text.p: Russian workers returned to the normal routine of waiting for long-delayed pay packets on Friday after a day of strikes and demonstrations marked by apathy and resignation.
Trade union leader Mikhail Shmakov said over 20 million people had joined Thursday's day of protests against massive wage and pension arrears, but it was not clear where his figures came from.
The interior ministry, basing its calculations on protest marches in Moscow and other cities, had put the number at just under two million.

President Boris Yeltsin, attending a summit of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), welcomed the peaceful course of the demonstrations, but said they illustrated the shortcomings of government actions so far.
"The president expects the new cabinet to take energetic and resolute steps to resolve social problems," Interfax news agency quoted Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky as saying.
"He is convinced that one such way is to continue the dialogue and cooperation between the government and the unions."

Yeltsin, who on Friday appointed Yastrzhembsky his deputy chief of staff, named a new government this month, giving leading roles to two young reformers in an attempt to revive stalled economic reforms.

His ministers have promised fast action to pay the bills and they admit wage arrears total more than 50 trillion roubles ($8.8 billion), including 10 trillion owed by the state. Some arrears have already been paid.

Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov told a news conference that his party -- the biggest force in the State Duma lower house of parliament -- was considering calling for a vote of no-confidence in the government after the demonstrations.

"Yesterday every citizen said 'no' to the economic course and 'no' to the current composition of the government," he said. "A question of no-confidence in the government not only remains on the agenda but is highly topical."
The Duma, fearful that Yeltsin would dissolve it if deputies voted no-confidence in the government, has backed away from such votes on previous occasions.

The wage arrears is one of Yeltsin's most obvious problems, but the Russian leader also faced an international audience within the CIS, a loose grouping of 12 former Soviet republics created after the superpower fell apart.
Friday's summit, postponed twice due to Yeltsin's prolonged absence with pneumonia and heart problems, was looking at ways to develop economic integration between the states.

"Our common opinion was that the movement toward each other will continue," Yeltsin told a concluding news conference. "We accepted the concept of the economic integration of the CIS, for the first time."

Yeltsin, fit again after months of heart problems followed by pneumonia, won a personal vote of confidence from Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma, who had been sharply critical of Russia's role in the CIS on the eve of the summit.
"I can definitely say that it was a different Boris Nikolayevich (Yeltsin) from the one at all the sessions up to now," Kuchma told the news conference.

Ukraine guards its new independence jealously and Kiev is one of the more sceptical members of the CIS, which groups all the former Soviet republics except the three Baltic states of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.
